rows.query: In which Python module is the function urljoin defined?

trace.evidence: urllib.parse. urljoin ( base , url , allow_fragments = True ) ¶: Construct a full (“absolute”) URL by combining a “base URL” ( base ) with another URL ( url ). Informally, this uses components of the base URL, in particular the addressing scheme, the network location and (part of) the path, to provide missing components in the relative URL. For example: >>> from urllib.parse import urljoin >>> urljoin ( 'http://www.cwi.nl/ %7E guido/Python.html' , 'FAQ.html' ) 'http://www.cwi.nl/%7Eguido/FAQ.html' The allow_fragments argument has the same meaning and default as for urlsplit() . Note If url is an absolute URL (that is, it starts with // or scheme:// ), the url ’s hostname and/or scheme will be present in the result. For example: >>> urljoin ( 'http://www.cwi.nl/ %7E guido/Python.html' , ... '//www.python.org/ %7E guido' ) 'http://www.python.org/%7Eguido' If you do not want that behavior, preprocess the url with urlsplit() and urlunsplit() , removing possible scheme and netloc parts. Warning Because an absolute URL may be passed as the url parameter, it is generally not secure to use urljoin with an attacker-controlled url . For example in, urljoin("https://website.com/users/", username) , if username can contain an absolute URL, the result of urljoin will be the absolute URL. Changed in version 3.5: Behavior updated to match the semantics defined in RFC 3986 .

top_candidates.evidence: text: Hi all, I’ve been working on CPython tooling and Python documentation translation and want to raise a gap I keep running into. I’d like to know whether the packaging community sees it the same way, and whether Core Metadata is the right place to address it. The problem Python packaging has standardised mechanisms for all of the following: Implementation identity at runtime - sys.implementation.name (PEP 421) Implementation-compatible wheel selection - implementation tags in wheel filenames (PEP 425) Implementation-specific dependencies implementation_name environment markers (PEP 508) Python version constraints Requires-Python in Core Metadata What’s missing is a distribution-level Core Metadata field declaring that a package only supports certain Python implementations. Why existing mechanisms don’t cover it Wheel tags handle this at the artifact level pip rejects an incompatible wheel based on its filename. But an sdist has no implementation tag. When an installer falls back to an sdist, there is no standard normative metadata signal that the package is incompatible with the running implementation. The user gets a build failure or runtime error instead of a clear rejection. Environment markers ( implementation_name == "cpython" in Requires-Dist ) describe when a dependency should be installed. They don’t describe whether the package itself is compatible with an implementation. These are different semantic layers. Trove classifiers ( Programming Language :: Python :: Implementation :: PyPy ) are descriptive. They communicate claims but are not a normative constraint that an installer uses to reject a candidate. Supported-Platform has existed since Core Metadata 1.1 but its semantics have never been specified. Its documented scope is OS and CPU for binary distributions - a different domain. I don’t think repurposing it is a good fit. Proposed direction A new optional Core Metadata field, provisionally Requires-Implementation , modelled on Requires-Python : [project] requires-python = ">=3.12" requires-implementation = ["cpython", "pypy"] Requires-Implementation: cpython Requires-Implementation: pypy Values correspond to sys.implementation.name (PEP 421). The set is open — no central registry needed. A missing field means no restriction; existing packages are unaffected. Concrete examples A package with CPython-internal assumptions ships only an sdist. A GraalPy user gets a confusing failure today. Requires-Implementation: cpython lets the installer reject the candidate before attempting a build. Some packages fail at the build step itself on incompatible implementations, before any wheel is produced. The incompatibility is known at the project level but there’s nowhere standard to declare it. Tools comparing behaviour across implementations need machine-readable declared compatibility, not just descriptive classifiers. Recent precedent PEP 794 (accepted September 2025, PEP 794 – Import Name Metadata | peps.python.org ) added Import-Name and Import-Namespace to Core Metadata so project-level information can be served by an index without inspecting individual artifacts explicitly because inferring from wheel contents doesn’t work for sdists. That’s structurally close to what I’m proposing. The Simple API’s data-core-metadata means no new transport mechanism is needed. Questions for the community I have a direction, not a finished design. I’d specifically like feedback on: Semantic layer Is Core Metadata the right place, or should this live somewhere else? Value representation , Simple list of strings, or a specifier syntax? Should version-qualified constraints be in scope now or deferred? Installer behaviour , MUST-reject or SHOULD-warn? Specified in Core Metadata or in installer behaviour specs? Wheel interaction , what happens if a package declares Requires-Implementation: cpython but publishes a py3-none-any wheel? Scope , should this initially be runtime-only, leaving build-environment constraints to a separate proposal? Supported-Platform — Leave it alone, or use this as an opportunity to finally clarify or deprecate it? What I’m not proposing PyPI rejecting uploads based on this field A closed registry of implementation names Any change to wheel compatibility tags Build-environment constraints There was a short discussion in January 2024 ( Python implementation in metadata ) about implementation metadata, which concluded that classifiers are the current answer. That thread was about forcing a particular implementation in a dev environment. This is different: I’m asking whether a package can declare its own runtime compatibility as a normative constraint for installer candidate selection, especially for sdists. Feedback very welcome, especially from pip, uv, PyPI/Warehouse, and PyPA maintainers. If the gap is real and this direction makes sense, I’ll write a formal PEP draft.
top_candidates.label: text
